problem.title: Large-scale document classification
problem.context: An insurer receives between two and eight million documents a day (scanned forms, e-mails, PDFs) and classifies each one into one of 60 claim types with an LLM-based classifier. Volume varies strongly over the year: storm season brings four times the usual load. Three teams use the results: claims handling, fraud investigation and analytics. The documents contain personal data.

requirements.text: Classify every incoming document into a claim type, with a confidence.
Deliver the results to the three consuming teams.
Send the documents the classifier is unsure about to human review, and use the reviewers' corrections to improve the classifier.
During storm season, at eight million documents a day, every document is classified within two hours of arrival.
When classification quality drops for one claim type (for example, after a form changes its layout), operators see it within one day.
The classification costs less than 0.2 cents per document on average over the year.
A consuming team can change how it processes the results without the other teams or the classifier having to change.
The documents contain personal data and may not leave the EU.
The classifier uses an LLM from the insurer's approved provider, in its EU region.

points.description: Documents land in EU object storage, with Kafka events triggering preprocessing, deduplication, OCR, and adjacent-text extraction. Autoscaled Kubernetes workers batch 20 small documents for an approved EU-region LLM using the versioned prompt, publish results with provenance to team consumer groups, and feed hourly analytics; low-confidence outputs enter review, while validated monthly example updates and monitoring/audits govern quality. Trade-off: This provides scalable, region-constrained processing, traceability, and feedback-driven improvement. It gives up prompt freshness between monthly updates and incurs review, audit, and warehouse overhead, with low-confidence results potentially delayed.

points.description: EU object storage emits Kafka upload events, which drive Kubernetes workers that scale from 4 to 120 according to backlog. Each worker groups 20 small documents for inference through the approved LLM provider’s EU region. Trade-off: This provides EU-oriented data handling, elastic throughput, and batching efficiency, but batching can add latency while groups fill, and large autoscaling ranges plus Kafka and Kubernetes introduce operational complexity and potentially high peak resource costs.

Each team consumes that topic using its own consumer group, allowing teams to receive the results independently while sharing work among their own consumers. Trade-off: This provides team-level isolation, independent consumption rates, and replay through Kafka offsets. It adds topic and consumer-group management overhead, and each team must maintain its own consumer and handle the resulting operational and storage costs.

Each month, the examples are replaced, and the updated prompt is deployed only after checking it against 2,000 reviewed documents. Trade-off: This provides targeted human correction and a substantial quality gate, but low-confidence cases require labelling and improvements may be delayed by the monthly replacement and validation cycle.

points.description: The system displays each claim’s review share and mean confidence, triggering an alert when the relevant measure doubles. Separately, it audits a random sample of 300 classifications every week to estimate classification quality. Trade-off: This combines continuous visibility and rapid anomaly detection with a recurring, broader quality check. It adds dashboard and review overhead, while the sample may miss rare errors and mean confidence can diverge from actual correctness.

points.description: Documents are uploaded to EU object storage, which publishes upload events to Kafka. A classifier consumes those events, retrieves the documents, and submits them to the approved LLM deployment in its EU region for classification. Trade-off: This supports decoupled, scalable ingestion and EU-region processing. It adds Kafka and storage integration and operational complexity, while limiting model choice to the approved provider and its EU-region offering.

points.description: The system sends classifications below 0.7 to a labelling queue, uses corrected documents to replace prompt examples monthly, and validates each revision against 2,000 reviewed documents before deployment. A dashboard tracks per-claim review share and mean confidence, triggers an alert when these double, and complements a weekly random audit of 300 classifications. Trade-off: This combines targeted human review, controlled prompt updates, and ongoing oversight, but high-confidence errors may escape review, monthly updates can lag, and the validation and weekly audit require substantial effort.

alternatives.name: Document classification as built
alternatives.summary: An EU hosted, event-driven LLM pipeline classifies documents, routes uncertain results to staff, and publishes results for independent team consumption. Prompt changes are based on corrections and quality is monitored per claim type.

choices.value_id: Intake: EU object storage with Kafka upload events
choices.reason: The EU location is forced by C1; object storage and Kafka are implementation choices that support durable, event-driven intake.
choices.solution_quote: Incoming documents land in an object storage bucket in the EU region, and each upload puts a message on a Kafka topic.

choices.value_id: Preprocessing: OCR, content-hash deduplication, and adjacent extracted text
choices.reason: Text extraction enables classification of scans and documents; deduplication and adjacent text are implementation choices, not explicitly required.
choices.solution_quote: A preprocessing service reads the topic, extracts the text (with OCR for scanned forms), removes duplicates by content hash and writes the text next to the document.

choices.value_id: Classifier runtime: Kubernetes workers autoscaled from 4 to 120 by Kafka backlog
choices.reason: Elastic workers support storm-season throughput, but the contrast cannot prove this range is required or sufficient, and peak cost is not measured.
choices.solution_quote: The number of classifier workers scales with the length of the Kafka topic's backlog, from 4 to 120.

choices.value_id: LLM: approved provider in its EU region
choices.reason: C2 explicitly requires the approved provider in its EU region; the EU endpoint also supports C1.
choices.solution_quote: A classifier service, running on Kubernetes, sends the text to the approved provider's LLM in its EU region.

choices.value_id: Prompt: 60 claim definitions and ten labelled examples
choices.reason: The prompt represents all claim types and examples to guide classification, but the number and format of examples are not required by the problem.
choices.solution_quote: The prompt lists the 60 claim types with a short definition and ten labelled examples, and asks for a claim type and a confidence between 0 and 1.

choices.value_id: Inference batching: batches of 20 small documents
choices.reason: Batching is intended to lower cost, with a possible latency cost; neither the batch size nor its cost and latency effects are measured.
choices.solution_quote: Small documents are sent in batches of 20 to reduce cost.

choices.value_id: Result provenance: prompt version and model name stored with each result
choices.reason: Version and model provenance help diagnose quality shifts, though the problem does not prescribe this metadata.
choices.solution_quote: Every result is stored with the prompt version and the model name that produced it.

choices.value_id: Result delivery: second Kafka topic with one consumer group per team
choices.reason: Independent consumption serves loose coupling; Kafka is a free choice among ways to provide that separation.
choices.solution_quote: Results go to a second Kafka topic. Each consuming team has its own consumer group and reads at its own pace;

choices.reason: This delivers results to analytics, but the hourly schedule and warehouse mechanism are not specified by the requirements.
choices.solution_quote: analytics also loads the topic into the data warehouse every hour.

choices.value_id: Human review: confidence below 0.7 enters labelling queue
choices.reason: Human review of uncertain cases is required, while 0.7 and the labelling tool are chosen details.
choices.solution_quote: Documents with a confidence below 0.7 go to a review queue in a labelling tool, where claims staff correct the claim type.

choices.value_id: Prompt learning: monthly replacement of examples with corrected documents
choices.reason: Using reviewer corrections is required; monthly full example replacement is a chosen update strategy.
choices.solution_quote: Every month the team replaces the prompt's examples with recent corrected documents,

choices.value_id: Prompt validation: check against 2,000 reviewed documents before switch
choices.reason: Validation can reduce regression risk, but the requirement does not set the check size or require this specific gate.
choices.solution_quote: and checks the new prompt against 2,000 reviewed documents before switching to it.

choices.value_id: Quality monitoring: per-claim review share and mean confidence dashboard with doubling alert
choices.reason: Per-claim signals support finding localized changes, but no stated timing or evidence shows the alert meets the one-day target.
choices.solution_quote: A dashboard shows, per claim type, the share of documents sent to review and the mean confidence; an alert fires when the share sent to review for a claim type doubles from one week to the next.

choices.value_id: Quality audit: weekly random sample of 300 classifications
choices.reason: The sample supplies a human quality check, but its frequency and size are not specified and it does not alone ensure one-day visibility.
choices.solution_quote: Each week, analysts review a random sample of 300 classified documents.

adrs.title: Scale document inference while keeping data in the EU
adrs.context: The system must classify every input with confidence, handle the seasonal peak, control average inference cost, and keep personal data within the EU while using the approved EU-region LLM.

options.name: EU event intake, elastic Kubernetes workers, and batched approved EU inference
values: Intake: EU object storage with Kafka upload events
Preprocessing: OCR, content-hash deduplication, and adjacent extracted text
Classifier runtime: Kubernetes workers autoscaled from 4 to 120 by Kafka backlog
LLM: approved provider in its EU region
Prompt: 60 claim definitions and ten labelled examples
Inference batching: batches of 20 small documents
pros: Processes scans and extracts usable text.
Backlog-based scaling responds to changing volume.
Batching is intended to reduce cost.
EU storage and approved EU inference meet the location and provider constraints.
cons: The worker range and batch size are not backed by throughput or cost measurements.
options.reason: The approved EU provider is forced by C2 and EU handling by C1. Event buffering, Kubernetes, the scaling range, prompt format, and batch size are implementation choices; throughput and cost targets remain unverified.

options.name: Fixed worker pool
values: Intake: EU object storage with Kafka upload events
Classifier runtime: fixed worker count
Inference batching: batches of 20 small documents
LLM: approved provider in its EU region
pros: Predictable worker capacity and potentially steadier peak compute spending.
cons: Does not add capacity as backlog grows during storm season.
options.reason: It weakens support for the peak-throughput requirement. The available information does not establish that a correctly sized fixed pool would miss the two-hour target, so the contrast does not prove autoscaling is strictly forced.

adrs.title: Publish results for independent team consumption
adrs.context: Claims handling, fraud investigation, and analytics all need results, and each team must be able to change its processing independently.

options.name: Shared Kafka results topic with team consumer groups
values: Result provenance: prompt version and model name stored with each result
Result delivery: second Kafka topic with one consumer group per team
Analytics delivery: hourly warehouse load
pros: Each team can consume at its own pace.
Consumer changes are isolated from the classifier and other teams.
Analytics receives a regular warehouse feed.
cons: Kafka topic and consumer operations add infrastructure and maintenance.
options.reason: Independent consumption is required by Q4; Kafka consumer groups and the hourly warehouse schedule are free choices. Stored provenance supports later diagnosis.

adrs.title: Route uncertain classifications into a correction loop
adrs.context: The classifier must return a claim type and confidence, send uncertain results to staff, and use corrections to improve future classifications.

options.name: Confidence threshold, staff labelling, monthly prompt examples, and pre-release check
values: Human review: confidence below 0.7 enters labelling queue
Prompt learning: monthly replacement of examples with corrected documents
Prompt validation: check against 2,000 reviewed documents before switch
pros: Staff corrections feed future prompt examples.
A fixed review threshold gives an explicit routing rule.
The prompt is checked before a new version is used.
cons: The threshold and monthly cadence may not match changing uncertainty or drift.
Review and validation create delay and staff effort.
options.reason: Reviewing uncertain items and using corrections are required by R3. The 0.7 cutoff, monthly cadence, replacement strategy, and sample size are freely selected parameters.

adrs.title: Watch quality by claim type
adrs.context: Operators need to notice when classification quality degrades for a particular claim type within one day.

options.name: Per-type dashboard, review-share alert, and weekly sample
values: Quality monitoring: per-claim review share and mean confidence dashboard with doubling alert
Quality audit: weekly random sample of 300 classifications
pros: Per-claim measures can reveal localized changes.
The weekly human sample checks a signal beyond model confidence.
cons: Review share and mean confidence are indirect quality measures.
Weekly comparison and sampling do not establish one-day detection.
options.reason: Per-type visibility supports Q2, but the solution does not demonstrate that the alert fires within one day. The selected indicators, doubling rule, sample size, and cadence are not forced by the requirement.
